panels.caption: Republic Broadcasting House. Twenty minutes from now, the whole Republic will be listening.

narrative.text: The oath is two hours old. The crowd has not fully dispersed — they are still in the square, still in the side streets, still talking about what they just witnessed. Vyktor has arranged a radio address. Twenty minutes from now, the entire Republic will be listening.
Every Chancellor addresses the nation after the ceremony. It is expected. What is not expected — what no one can predict — is what you say.
You sit before the microphone. The broadcast engineer holds up three fingers. Two. One.
Sixty thousand people heard you take the oath. Twenty million will hear this.

choices.text: Speak of unity. Veltria has been divided long enough.
Speak of change. The old ways end today.
Speak of strength. Veltria will not be intimidated.

narrative.text: The red light blinks on. You lean forward.

Citizens of the Republic. I will not pretend today is a normal day. It is not. For twenty-three years this nation was governed by fear — fear of the wrong word, fear of the wrong friend, fear of the knock on the door at three in the morning. That era is over. Not because I say so. Because you said so. You stood in the cold this morning. Sixty thousand of you. And you made it so.
Through the glass partition you can see the broadcast engineer. She has stopped writing notes. She is just listening.

I know what divides us. I am not going to pretend otherwise. There are people in this Republic who voted for me and people who did not. There are people who are afraid of what comes next and people who cannot wait. I am asking both of them — all of you — for one thing. Not agreement. Not silence. Time. Give this government time to show you what it is made of. Judge us by what we do. Hold us to it.
You pause. In the silence you can hear the hum of the equipment, the distant sound of traffic outside. The whole Republic is in that silence.

Veltria is not a broken country. It is a country that was broken by bad leadership. There is a difference. We are still here. We are still capable of something extraordinary. I believe that. I would not be sitting in this chair if I did not believe it. Thank you.
The red light blinks off. Eleven minutes and forty seconds.
The phones are already ringing. Four to one positive. That is — unusual.
He says it like a man who has spent twenty years being suspicious of good news. But he is almost smiling.
The Halvekist bloc will call it sentimental. Let them. The rest of the country heard something different.
The red light blinks on. You have fourteen minutes. You use every one of them.

Citizens of the Republic. I am going to speak plainly because I think you have earned plain speaking. The last government stole from you. Not metaphorically. Not as a manner of expression. They stole pensions, contracts, judicial appointments, your children's futures. I have the files. I have read them. And I am telling you today — in my first hour as your Chancellor — that this stops.
In the booth, Vyktor's expression does not change. But his pen has stopped moving.

In the next thirty days this government will do three things. We will open the BNI files to an independent commission. We will restore the pension adjustments that were frozen in 1959. And we will begin the process of returning what was taken. I will not give you a timeline that I cannot keep. I will give you a commitment that I will keep. The Republic belongs to its people. Not to the people in this building. To you.
There is a sound — not applause, the studio is empty — but something. A kind of exhale across the whole country. You can almost feel it.

To those who built their lives around the old arrangements — I am not your enemy. But I am not your protector either. The law will apply to everyone now. That is not a threat. That is the definition of a Republic. Thank you.
The red light blinks off. Vyktor opens the booth door.
You named the pension freeze.
The finance ministry is going to have a very difficult morning. So will we. But — the response lines are overwhelmed. We did not have enough operators.
He pauses. A complicated expression crosses his face — something between professional concern and something more human.
My mother had her pension frozen. She never said anything. I did not know she knew why.
The red light blinks on. Nine minutes. You do not need more.

Citizens of the Republic. Our neighbors are watching. They have been watching since the votes were counted. Some of them are hoping we are distracted. Some of them are hoping the transition creates an opening — an opening for pressure, for interference, for the kind of quiet manipulation that has shaped this region for forty years. I want to address them directly.
Through the glass, Vyktor straightens in his chair.

Veltria's borders are not negotiable. Veltria's sovereignty is not negotiable. Veltria's right to govern itself according to its own constitution — not according to anyone else's preferences — is not negotiable. We seek no conflict. We will not manufacture one. But we will not apologize for existing, and we will not mistake patience for weakness.
You let the silence sit for a moment. Three seconds. Five. Long enough to mean something.
To the citizens of this Republic — you have a government today that is not afraid. I want you to feel that. I want you to carry it with you. We have work to do. Let us begin. Thank you.
The red light blinks off. Nine minutes and twelve seconds. Vyktor opens the booth door immediately.
You addressed Tyvaren without naming them.

Their embassy will have filed a report within the hour. The Iron Covenant people will be pleased. The Foreign Ministry will be — less pleased. But the polling on national security is going to be favorable.
He considers for a moment.
For what it is worth — I believed it. The part about not mistaking patience for weakness. I believed that.
